title: Galois Group of the cos(20°) Minimal Polynomial has Order 3
description: Proves that the Galois group of 8X³ − 6X − 1 over ℚ has cardinality 3. The polynomial 8X³ − 6X − 1 is the minimal polynomial of cos(20°), and its irreducibility over ℚ is established via Eisenstein's criterion applied to the shifted polynomial X³ − 6X² + 9X − 3. Since all three roots (cos(20°), cos(100°), cos(220°)) are polynomial expressions in any single root, the splitting field equals ℚ(α) with [ℚ(α):ℚ] = 3, giving |Gal| = 3. This eliminates the cos20_gal_order axiom used in AngleTrisectionOQ02.

overview.historicalContext:
The polynomial 8X³ − 6X − 1 arises from the triple-angle formula cos(3θ) = 4cos³θ − 3cosθ with θ = 20°: setting θ = 20° gives 4cos³(20°) − 3cos(20°) = cos(60°) = 1/2, and clearing denominators yields 8x³ − 6x − 1. The three roots cos(20°), cos(100°), cos(220°) correspond to the three angles 3θ ≡ 60° (mod 360°).

Pierre Wantzel (1837) was the first to prove rigorously that trisecting a 60° angle is impossible with compass and straightedge. His argument: a real number is constructible iff its minimal polynomial over ℚ has degree a power of 2. Since 8x³ − 6x − 1 is irreducible over ℚ (degree 3, not a power of 2), cos(20°) is not constructible, and 20° cannot be obtained from 60° by ruler-and-compass construction.

Évariste Galois (1832, published posthumously 1846) developed the theory connecting polynomial irreducibility to symmetry groups. The Galois group of 8x³ − 6x − 1 over ℚ is ℤ/3ℤ: cyclic of order 3, confirming the three roots are all conjugate and the extension ℚ ⊂ ℚ(cos 20°) has no proper intermediate fields. This file provides a complete Lean 4 machine-checked proof, eliminating the cos20_gal_order axiom previously assumed in AngleTrisectionOQ02.lean.
overview.problemStatement: Determine |Gal(8X³ − 6X − 1 / ℚ)|. The key steps are: (1) prove 8X³ − 6X − 1 is irreducible over ℚ; (2) show all three roots lie in ℚ(α) for any root α, so the splitting field equals ℚ(α); (3) conclude [SplittingField : ℚ] = [ℚ(α) : ℚ] = 3 and hence |Gal| = 3.
overview.proofStrategy: Irreducibility is proved by shifting: the substitution Y = 2X + 2 transforms 8X³ − 6X − 1 into X³ − 6X² + 9X − 3, which is Eisenstein at p = 3 (coefficients −6, 9, −3 divisible by 3; constant term −3 not divisible by 9; leading coefficient 1 not divisible by 3). Irreducibility transfers back via the invertible linear change of variables. For the Galois group: the key algebraic identities show that if α is a root then β = 2α² − α − 1 and γ = 1 − 2α² are also roots (verified by ring). Since all roots are polynomial expressions in α, adjoin(α) splits p, giving [SplittingField : ℚ] = 3. From this, |Gal| = 3 follows from Mathlib's Polynomial.Gal.card_of_separable.
keyInsights: The Eisenstein criterion on X³ − 6X² + 9X − 3 at p = 3 gives irreducibility over ℤ; Gauss's lemma lifts to ℚ
Irreducibility transfers through the invertible substitution X ↦ (Y−2)/2 via composition with the inverse linear map
The factored form 8a³−6a−1 = 8(a−α)(a−β)(a−γ) is a pure ring identity, holding in any commutative ring
Since all roots of p lie in ℚ(α), the splitting field has degree exactly 3 over ℚ

From degree 3 splitting: |Gal| divides 3! = 6 (from permutation action on roots) and is divisible by 3 (since p is irreducible of prime degree), so |Gal| = 3. Moreover, a group of prime order 3 must be cyclic (ℤ/3ℤ), which means the extension ℚ ⊂ ℚ(cos 20°) has no proper intermediate fields — ruling out any step-by-step compass-and-straightedge construction that would require a tower of degree-2 extensions.

conclusion.summary: This file provides a complete machine-verified proof that |Gal(8X³−6X−1/ℚ)| = 3. The proof proceeds entirely by algebra: Eisenstein criterion, linear substitution irreducibility transfer, explicit root expressions, and Mathlib's splitting field theory. No geometric or transcendental reasoning is used. The result eliminates the cos20_gal_order axiom from AngleTrisectionOQ02.
conclusion.implications: The cyclic Galois group of order 3 confirms that the splitting field of the cos(20°) polynomial is a degree-3 extension of ℚ with Galois group ℤ/3ℤ. This is consistent with the impossibility of trisecting 60° by compass and straightedge (degree not a power of 2) and with the possibility using a marked ruler (degree divides 2⁰ · 3¹). The proof technique — Eisenstein on a shifted polynomial, then transfer via invertible linear change of variables — is a useful pattern applicable to other cubics.
openQuestions: The gallery siblings angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-01 and oq-03 prove |Gal| = 3 for cos(π/7) and cos(40°) using the same Eisenstein-shift technique. Can a unified Lean 4 proof handle all cos(2π/p) minimal polynomials for prime p ≥ 3 with a single parametric theorem, using Chebyshev polynomial structure?
Is there a Mathlib path to the Kronecker-Weber theorem that would let one classify all abelian extensions of ℚ and prove, as a corollary, that [Q(cos(2π/n)):Q] = φ(n)/2 for all n ≥ 3?

The proof establishes |Gal| = 3 via cardinality, but does not exhibit an explicit automorphism σ: Q(α) → Q(α) with σ(α) = β = 2α²-α-1 and σ³ = id. Formalizing this generator would make the abelian structure of Gal(8X³-6X-1/Q) ≅ Z/3Z explicit in Lean.

sections.title: Background: Triple-Angle Formula and Proof Strategy
sections.summary: Module-level comment explaining that p = 8X³−6X−1 is the minimal polynomial of cos(20°), arising from cos(3×20°) = 1/2. States the two key algebraic identities showing β = 2α²−α−1 and γ = 1−2α² are the other roots. Cites Wantzel (1837) and describes how once all roots are in ℚ(α), the Galois group has order 3.

sections.title: Part I: Algebraic Identities — Root Images of α
sections.summary: Proves three ring identities (root_image_beta, root_image_gamma, quadratic_cofactor_root) establishing that if α is a root of 8x³−6x−1, then β = 2α²−α−1 and γ = 1−2α² are also roots. All proofs use the ring tactic to factor the identity as a product involving 8a³−6a−1, then substitute the root hypothesis.

sections.title: Parts II and II-B: Polynomial Properties and Irreducibility
sections.summary: Defines p = 8X³−6X−1 and proves its basic properties (degree, non-zero). The Eisenstein shift q = X³−6X²+9X−3 is introduced and proved irreducible over ℤ by Eisenstein's criterion at p=3, then over ℚ by Gauss's lemma. The substitution q(2X+2) = p is verified, and irreducibility transfers to p via the invertible linear change of variables (with explicit inverse X ↦ X/2−1 composed through comp_assoc).

sections.title: Parts III–V: Splitting Field Analysis
sections.summary: Constructs root_in_sf (a root of p in the splitting field), verifies β and γ lie in ℚ(α) (as polynomial expressions), and proves the factored form 8a³−6a−1 = 8(a−α)(a−β)(a−γ). Uses this to show all roots of p are in ℚ(α) (rootSet_subset_adjoin), hence ℚ(α) = SplittingField (adjoin_root_eq_top). The finrank equals 3 because the minpoly of α has degree 3 (since p is irreducible and p(α) = 0). Also establishes the divisibility bounds 3 ∣ |Gal| ∣ 6.

sections.title: Part VI: Main Result — |Gal| = 3
sections.summary: cos20_gal_card: applies Polynomial.Gal.card_of_separable to conclude |Gal(8X³−6X−1/ℚ)| = [SplittingField:ℚ] = 3. Also exposes trisection_poly_irreducible as a public interface for the irreducibility of p. These results eliminate the cos20_gal_order axiom from AngleTrisectionOQ02.lean.

Cardano's cubic formula (Wiedijk #37) applies to 8X³−6X−1: since the Galois group $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ of order 3 is solvable, $\cos(20°)$ IS expressible by radicals — the radical formula gives the roots via cube roots of complex numbers (the casus irreducibilis where all three roots are real yet the cube root formula requires complex intermediate steps). The impossibility result in this entry is compass-and-straightedge constructibility (requires a degree-2 power tower), which is strictly stronger than radical inexpressibility.

Galois's solvability criterion: a root is expressible by radicals iff its Galois group is solvable. This entry proves $|\text{Gal}(8X^3-6X-1/\mathbb{Q})| = 3 \Rightarrow \text{Gal} \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$, which is abelian hence solvable. By the solvability criterion, $\cos(20°)$ IS expressible by radicals (Cardano applies) — the angle trisection impossibility is about the stronger requirement of compass-and-straightedge constructibility (towers of degree-2 extensions), not radical expressibility.

references.note: First rigorous proof that angle trisection and cube doubling are impossible with compass and straightedge, by showing the relevant minimal polynomials have degree not a power of 2. This entry formalizes the key step: |Gal(minpoly(cos 20°)/ℚ)| = 3, so [ℚ(cos 20°):ℚ] = 3, which is not a power of 2.
